# A target with no answer for sngl:async refuses the build, at the call.
#
# The two ids are declared now, so a program can write them -- and what a
# target that cannot emit one produced was neither an error nor working code.
# bubbletea's Go emitter had already spelled the call as a method on the model,
# so `async.post` there emitted `m.post(func(){...})` and the first anyone heard
# of it was the Go compiler reporting an undefined method, with no position in
# the SNGL that asked for it. RequireIntrinsicFallback is the guard for exactly
# this and never saw the call: a backend consults it at the generic path, which
# that spelling had already left.
#
# A txtar rather than a golden because a golden runs nothing and this is a
# refusal: the claim is the exit status and the text, which is the CLI's to make.

# post is answered on the platform axis, and bubbletea owns its loop: nothing
# outside Update may touch the model, which is the same reason it cannot take
# an effect timer.
! sngl generate --platform bubbletea --lang go -o out post.sngl
stderr 'async.post runs a closure back on the thread the target draws on'
stderr 'bubbletea has no way to reach one'
# The call's own line, not the enclosing statement's: allBlocks hands over a
# view body before the handler bodies hanging off it, so the position used to
# come out as the button rather than the post inside its @click.
stderr 'post.sngl:13:'
! stderr 'post.sngl:12:'
! stderr 'panic'

# spawn is answered on the language axis, so a different program is refused for
# a different reason and names the other half of the build.
! sngl generate --platform html --lang none -o out spawn.sngl
stderr 'async.spawn runs a closure without waiting for it'
stderr 'has no way to start one'
! stderr 'panic'

# A platform has the last word over the language. html's client handlers are
# JavaScript whatever --lang says, so Go answering async.spawn is not html
# answering it: this emitted a bare `spawn(...)` into the inline script, an
# undefined identifier and a ReferenceError at click time -- the same failure
# as bubbletea's `m.post(...)`, reached along the other axis.
! sngl generate --platform html --lang go -o out spawngo.sngl
stderr 'go on html has no way to start one'
! stderr 'panic'

# The interpreter answers both, which is not a refusal at all: `sngl test` runs
# the checked IR with no lowering, so passAsyncCapable never speaks there and a
# program naming the package got "unsupported method" from the evaluator with
# no position. One thread means both ids are the same thing -- call it -- and a
# test wants the closure to have run before the assertion does.
sngl test interp.sngl
stdout '0 failures'

# And the target that does answer builds, so the refusal is about the target
# rather than about the declaration.
sngl generate --platform fyne --lang go -o out post.sngl
grep 'fyne.Do' out/model.go

-- post.sngl --
import ui "sngl:ui"
import async "sngl:async"

output {
    go {
        fyne
    }
}

ui.window(title="t") {
    var n = 0
    ui.button(text="go", @click {
        async.post(func() {
            n = n + 1
        })
    })
}
-- interp.sngl --
import ui "sngl:ui"
import async "sngl:async"
import test "sngl:test"

output {
    none {
        html
    }
}

func testBothRun(t test.Test) {
    var hits = 0
    async.post(func() {
        hits = hits + 1
    })
    async.spawn(func() {
        hits = hits + 1
    })
    t.assert(hits == 2)
}

ui.window(title="t") {
    ui.text(value="x")
}
-- spawngo.sngl --
import ui "sngl:ui"
import async "sngl:async"

output {
    go {
        html
    }
}

ui.window(title="t") {
    var n = 0
    ui.button(text="go", @click {
        async.spawn(func() {
            n = n + 1
        })
    })
}
-- spawn.sngl --
import ui "sngl:ui"
import async "sngl:async"

output {
    none {
        html
    }
}

ui.window(title="t") {
    var n = 0
    ui.button(text="go", @click {
        async.spawn(func() {
            n = n + 1
        })
    })
}
